title: Friends of other faiths
hookLine: friendship across faiths, each keeping their own
tomorrow: a fight against Moses. why does the Mishnah leave Moses out?

cards: Pizza boxes on the stage after closing night. Owen came, who grew up Lutheran, and Yasmin from the crew, who is Muslim. What does each keep?
Their own. And late in the night, the questions get real. Owen asks: so what do you actually think happens to me?
It's easier to change the subject. The Talmud keeps a friendship built on questions like that, between Rabbi Judah the Prince and a Roman it calls Antoninus. One day Antoninus brings a hard one.
After death, he says, body and soul can both get off. The body says: the soul did it. The soul says: the body did it.

teach.b: Rabbi Judah answers the way friends do: with a story. A king has an orchard of fine early figs, and he sets two guards, one who can't walk and one who can't see. The one who can't walk says: I see beautiful figs.
So he rides on the shoulders of the one who can't see, and together they eat the figs. The king comes back. The first says: me?
I have no legs. The second says: me? I have no eyes.
So the king sets one on the other's shoulders and judges them together. Body and soul, the rabbi says, answer as one. Now notice what the scene doesn't do.

teach.h: NOBODY ASKS THE OTHER TO SWITCH.
teach.b: Nobody asks the other to switch. The question is real, the answer is real, and the Talmud tells other talks between the two of them as well.

Another page of the Talmud puts this kind of friendship to work: support the poor of other peoples along with your own, visit their sick, bury their dead, because of darkhei shalom, the ways of peace.
In that picture, friendship across faiths isn't pretending you agree. It's honesty about where you stand, and showing up anyway.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's answer to a Roman's hardest question is a story about two guards stealing figs.

how: Jewish tradition keeps stories of friendship across faiths, like Rabbi Judah the Prince and the Roman Antoninus trading questions, and the Talmud teaches caring for the poor, the sick and the dead of other peoples because of the ways of peace.

games.q: what does “friends of other faiths” mean?
o: a friendship across faiths, each keeping their own
a group where people of all faiths pray as one
a promise to treat every belief as the same

games.q: a rabbi, a Roman, an orchard — tap the pairs.
p: a Roman who asks the rabbi real questions
one can't walk, one can't see

s: the Talmud tells of a rabbi and a Roman who traded hard questions
Rabbi Judah the Prince and Antoninus; one talk ends with the parable of the orchard.
friendship across faiths means agreeing it's all the same
each keeps their own; the honesty is what makes it a friendship.
the Talmud says to visit only the sick of your own community
Gittin 61a: visit the sick of other peoples too, because of the ways of peace.

games.q: a friend from another faith is out sick for a week. your crowd is mostly from your own community, and nobody's been by. what fits the ways of peace?
o: visit her, the way you'd visit anyone from your own crowd.
send a card; visiting is really for your own community's sick.
wait until her own faith community has visited first.
games.why: the Talmud says to visit the sick of other peoples along with your own, because of darkhei shalom, the ways of peace.

practice: Open a message to a friend whose faith, or lack of one, isn't yours. Write one honest question you've never asked them, about something they keep and why it matters to them.
Read it once, then send it, or save it for when you're face to face.

wordCard.voice: Friends of other faiths: a friendship across a line of belief, where each keeps their own and the questions stay honest.

orig.note: Hebrew: the ways of peace; the Talmud's reason for caring for neighbors of every people.

carryVoice: Keep this: friends across faiths. Two guards, one orchard, each carrying the other a little. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 91a-b (Antoninus asks about body and soul; Rabbi's parable of the lame and the blind guards in the king's orchard)
Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 10a-b (other conversations between Rabbi and Antoninus)
Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 61a (support the poor of the nations with the poor of Israel, visit their sick, bury their dead, because of the ways of peace)
